MR. LUNDRIGAN-FAILURE OF MINISTERS TO RESPOND IN ADJOURNMENT DEBATE-MOTION TO REFER TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The matter I am about to raise involves the privileges of all hon. members of this house. For several months the members of my party have been directing questions to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) about development programs to be introduced for Newfoundland. To those questions we have had inconsistent and conflicting replies. I therefore gave notice that I would raise a certain matter on the late show, hoping to inform the minister of the crisis facing Newfoundland and of the serious unemployment situation which has reached emergency proportions. I wanted to suggest short term programs which might help the province.
On coming here last night I found the minister absent. In fact, just before ten o'clock I was advised by the parliamentary secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Forest) that the minister would not be present in the house, being somewhere else. Neither was the first nor the second acting minister, if one may use that term, present in the house. I therefore feel that there has been a breach of privilege.
As Your Honour has so often said, the value of the late show is that it enables hon. members with grievances or questions to bring forward their subject matters at the time of adjournment. A responsible member of the government will listen to those grievances or questions, and reply. Of course, since we have a roster system under which not all ministers are present in the house at one time, it is very difficult for hon. members to address their questions to appropriate
bring forward their subject matters at the time of adjournment.
Having checked the record, Mr. Speaker, I contend that our late show procedure is unsatisfactory. Since there seems to be poor rapport between hon. members of this house and members of the cabinet so far as the late show is concerned, making it impossible for important matters to be discussed adequately and responsibly on the late show, and since the privileges of all members of the house are being curtailed by the ways in which our rules are being dishonoured by some, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath)-
-that the Committee on Procedure and Organization inquire into the operation of the rules relating to Standing Order 26, Standing Order 39(5), Standing Order 39(6), and Standing Order 40, and the roster system of ministerial attendance in the house; recommend revision of these standing orders and practices for the greater flow of administrative information to this house; and report back to this house by Friday, June 20.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of us get used to seeing a familiar scene without noticing that something is missing. Many have never realized that this House of Commons, the very seat of Canadian government, is devoid of the national flag of our country. If any place in Canada is worthy of being arrayed by the flag surely the Houses of Parliament are.
Those of us who have visited national assemblies in other countries could not help but notice the prominent display of national flags in their chambers. Even the provincial legislatures I have visited in Canada display

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to ensure that a person has the right to know what information about himself is collected and made available to others for a fee. The purpose of this bill is to make this information available to the person concerned.

VANCOUVER-CONTINUATION OF FREEZE ON URBAN RENEWAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct this question to the Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing. As he knows, 1 personally am opposed to special privileges and discrimination. Because of the urgency of the matter may I ask the minister whether he will advise us why urban renewal projects and public housing in Vancouver have not been unfrozen, as have some in Ontario, and will he please tell us when he anticipates they will be taken out of the deep freeze in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: VANCOUVER-CONTINUATION OF FREEZE ON URBAN RENEWAL
speechtext: Perhaps the question should be allowed, but I think I should remind the hon. member that we are now considering the very subject to which the hon. member's question refers, and it may be that the matter might be raised later on during the day. In any event I will allow the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):
subtopic: VANCOUVER-CONTINUATION OF FREEZE ON URBAN RENEWAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no attempt whatsoever to be discriminatory in dealing with either public housing projects or urban renewal projects. Certain of the public housing projects, which were delayed in an attempt to evaluate them in terms of their social and physical characteristics, have been released recently, indeed within the last few days. To my knowledge no specific project for the city of Vancouver has been held up.
With regard to the urban renewal matter, I am reviewing this as quickly as possible. I am not in a position to make any definitive statement at this time but hope to give a clear statement within a matter of weeks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that I have an unusually large audience in the house for the continuation of the debate on the housing bill. Hon. members will recall that at the last occasion, on Wednesday before six o'clock, I lauded the minister and congratulated him on his good intentions to do something about housing. I also pointed out to him that he had to contend with an arm that he would trust to execute his desires, namely the C.M.H.C., which was not exactly in keeping with an efficient organization. Indeed, I pointed out that in the field of research their contribution had been nil. As mortgage guarantors they do not even do the job that private mortgage companies are doing. Private companies are lending more money with easier terms, so the comparison is certainly not in their favour.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I have indicated that I am completely in favour of the minister's desire, through the medium of this new bill, to promote construction of low rental or limited dividend housing. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister that last year I was asked to help a group in Toronto build a limited dividend project consisting of 600 units in the heart of the city, almost within walking distance of downtown. The proposed rents ranged from $75 for a bachelor apartment to $130 for a two bedroom apartment.
The answer I received from C.M.H.C. was to this effect: "Well, Mr. Otto, those rents are much too high". As I say, this was last year when the welfare department was paying $156 a month minimum for the worst type of accommodation. So I asked a gentleman in C.M.H.C.: "On what figures do you base your statement that the rents are too high?" He replied: "We have some figures compiled in 1957". I was absolutely dumbfounded with that answer, but that is typical of their attitude.

Again, Mr. Speaker, at a later time I presented a critique on Habitat '67, a project that I think was wonderful, an idea that could be expanded a great deal, and their answer to me was, quoting directly from their letter:
First C.M.H.C. does not have a large stake in Habitat '67 either financially or from a prestige standpoint. Our financial contribution was the sum of $250,000 which was earmarked for research after the completion of the structure. We have no responsibility for the design or concept of Habitat '67 f
In other words, what C.M.H.C. is saying in this letter is that they are not interested in Habitat '67. They are not interested in promoting research or in granting money for that purpose in order to get Habitat '67 to conform to Canadian building standards.
All in all, I should like to say this about my experience with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This is not at all personal because I have had a great deal of gentlemanly attention from and have conducted some good negotiations with these people. I like them and I know the minister will like them. But when he analyses the situation coldly, I think he will find that C.M.H.C. is a dead duck. The corporation is absolutely useless in most of the fields in which it is empowered to act.
What is needed is a complete shakeup in C.M.H.C. Retire those who want to be retired. Get rid of the dead wood-yes, let us call it dead wood-and get a new organization. The minister is not going to get very far with the organization he now has.
If the minister wants to hear some ideas, I have 76 pages of ideas on how C.M.H.C. could improve its contribution to home construction. If the minister wonders why C.M.H.C. still has to come back to the house and ask for an increase of another few million dollars for guaranteeing mortgages, let me inform the minister that every other organization bases their guarantee on the loss ratio. In the mortgage field, as guarantor you have no loss. C.M.H.C. could easily guarantee twice as much as they are presently guaranteeing.
On Wednesday I spoke of the problem of getting National Housing Act money into areas outside Toronto and other large municipalities. This could be done by helping in the matter of administration and collection. I also spoke about C.M.H.C.'s failure even to grasp ideas concerning research, whether on sewage disposal or other types of land development. Perhaps the minister will ask C.M.H.C. why it is they demand an assurance that some lending institution is willing to put up money before the loan is guaranteed. It
May 30, 1969

does not make sense. If C.M.H.C. say that they will guarantee the money themselves, then a lot more lending institutions will compete in the mortgage field. At the present time lending institutions are actually making money just by giving some indication that they are interested.
The matter of legal fees was brought up by the former minister and his task force, and this is another area where the problem is easy to solve. Both the minister and C.M.H.C. know that every title has already been searched before they grant a mortgage on property. Why does the corporation not simply state that every piece of property mortgaged under the national housing legislation automatically has title insurance? As soon as the worry over title is removed and the title is guaranteed, legal fees will go down from $600 or $700 per house to about $25 because there is no need for lawyers. The solution is so easy; yet they cannot seem to see it.
On the question of assistance to provincial housing corporations I am sure-and I have explored this question with the hon. Mr. Randall and others-that if vendors could be given a national housing or C.M.H.C. guarantee-in different form, mind you-all types of buildings could be purchased. Vendors seldom receive very much money down, so if the Ontario Housing Corporation could give the vendor a bond based on the rent and buy the property which would be guaranteed by the government of Canada, then the vendor would be only too happy to sell. Even though he does not get one nickel down he does get a guarantee. With this he will be able to negotiate with a bank if he wants any additional cash.
There is one last matter on which I do not want to dwell because I have spoken to the minister about it. The minister will probably rise to the defence of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because this seems to be the loyal thing to do. If C.M.H.C. were a department of government, I would not blame him for rising to their defence. But let me remind him that C.M.H.C. is a crown corporation, not the minister's department. He does not have to defend the corporation blindly.
Therefore, I suggest to the minister that he look at this establishment carefully, despite all the nice attention he receives from the gentlemen in charge. I think he will find that if Parkinson's law has set into any corporation it is well entrenched in C.M.H.C. Even Peter's law is well entrenched. It is a corporation that has little use at the moment. It is
National Housing Act
dead. It is stagnant. Yet it could be very powerful and influential and of great assistance to the minister. But the minister must shake it up. He must get rid of the dead wood and promote men who are ambitious, men who are keen to grasp new ideas. Otherwise all the good intentions that the minister has expressed, which I believe are well founded, having known the minister and his desires for many years, will come to nothing. What he requires behind him is an arm that will be efficient, that will do something and make its existence worth while.

Mr. Speaker, may I join other hon. members who have spoken in offering my good wishes to the new minister in the work he has taken up. I believe a good start has been made. For the first time in living memory housing is not being treated as an "etcetera" of another department. It has been pried loose and is not to be considered as falling within the purview of a department unrelated to housing. I believe housing has come under five different ministries within the last ten years. Now housing is to be the responsibility of one minister. Soon I hope we shall have a full-time minister of housing, and I hope the present minister will become the full-time minister of housing and urban affairs. The field of housing is most important and ought to be the responsibility of a full-time portfolio.
I know that before the minister assumed his new responsibilities he took an immersion course in housing. I hope he was totally immersed. I hope he went deeply enough into the subject to gain a real insight into the problems. I hope he gained a knowledge of the housing needs of people with incomes of less than $6,500 a year. The problem increases in intensity for those earning less than that amount.
The housing problem is really not a problem of housing but one of income. Those with high enough incomes can obtain houses. Consequently the problem of housing is to provide homes for those whose incomes will not permit them to obtain their own homes. That is where the real housing problem lies.
I hope the minister feels that the time has come to stop talking and start building homes. Here may I say that I do not share the view of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto), who has just spoken, that the minister will have to be under the dictates of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
the minister is determined to build low cost houses and public low rent housing I submit he can assert his authority even over Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In my view ministerial determination is required if the right priorities are to be pursued. The corporation must be given the sinews of war. It must be given the authority and the money to do the job. There must be proper directives and proper co-operation with the provinces. I think the minister's first test will be in achieving that co-operation.
When we talk about homes being built we must ask ourselves, what kind of homes are they to be and for whom are they to be built? The minister said that the primary objective of the government is to provide decent houses for all Canadians. But, Mr. Speaker, by concentrating on that broad objective I submit that we are not focusing our attention sharply enough on the areas of greatest need.
Last year I attended the housing conference held in the city of Toronto. Over 500 delegates from all over Canada found that it was necessary for the government to lay down much more specific guidelines and directives than had previously been laid down. Guideline No. 6 of that conference was:
As long as government allocations for housing are insufficient, priority within housing budgets should go to helping those with the greatest need.
I am quoting from a pamphlet published by the Canadian Welfare Council. The pamphlet goes on to say:
The quantitative implications of such a policy have been estimated to be in the neighbourhood of 20,000-30,000 low-income dwellings a year requiring an investment of public funds of about $300 million annually-or about two to three times the best we have been able to achieve in any one year so far.
That will be a primary consideration for the minister. It is not good enough for the minister to say that we must provide decent housing for all Canadians. We must begin thinking specifically about the needs of certain Canadians, those with modest or low incomes. I am thinking of those who earn $6,500 a year and less. If we are to consider their needs we must close our ears and not listen to complaints from those people belonging to the group which has been mainly assisted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the past. If the minister can close his ears and not listen to their complaints, if he will make a determined effort to attain the objective I have outlined, and if he will give adequate direction to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, then I think

that priority No. 1, the provision of housing for our low income groups, will be met. The minister must take this objective seriously. In February the Canadian Welfare Council stated:
Continuing research, limited dividend projects, non-profit and co-operative housing, acquisition of existing dwellings in scattered sites, and income supplements are all desirable parts of a comprehensive housing program, and the task force is to be commended for recognizing this; but to put them forward at this time as substitutes for public housing is grossly misleading.
I wish to emphasize the importance of such statements. Today I am speaking on behalf of those who must have public housing. I know how important limited dividend housing is and how necessary it is to renovate older homes. Nevertheless, if we are to begin to tackle priority No. 1 we must provide adequate public, low rent housing for our people. In my view this is a must and comes before everything else.
I have already indicated that the Canadian Welfare Council contends that we must build a minimum of between 20,000 and 30,000 low income dwellings every year. That is two or three times the 10,000 dwellings we now build each year. The public housing stock of Canada makes up less than 1 per cent of our total housing stock. On the other hand, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) pointed out yesterday, 30 per cent of Britain's total housing stock consists of public housing. That ratio will not be achieved easily in this country. If we are to work toward its attainment the minister will have to apply concentrated attention to public housing needs and pay no attention to anything else. I do not know whether he is prepared to do that but he must do so if our housing crisis is to be overcome.
The report of the Task Force on Housing states that 100,0000 families across Canada are on waiting lists for public housing. I would point out that many other families needing public housing have concluded that it is useless to be on any waiting list. Some time ago in Vancouver I inquired about vacancies in a certain public housing project. The manager of the project told me that only death can create vacancies there. Some people think the public housing situation is so hopeless that they do not bother even to place their names on waiting lists. I was therefore glad to hear the minister announce that at least half a dozen projects would be taken out of the deep freeze. I was glad to hear that this is to happen in Toronto but was less than

reassured to hear that it will be several weeks or even months before the minister can make a similar announcement with respect to the smaller and medium size centres of Canada.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), asked the minister this morning when Vancouver's two big housing and urban development projects will be taken out of the deep freeze. He could obtain no information other than the reply of the minister already publicized that it will be some weeks before that is done. I point out that since November authorities of the city of Vancouver have pleaded with the minister in charge of housing and with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to take these big projects out of the deep freeze in order that they may be proceeded with. The people of Vancouver are in desperate need of the Strathcona area development and the downtown project No. 4A. This would be the beginning. To have to wait for weeks is just too much. Something ought to be done to cut the red tape and defeat Parkinson's law, if that is what is doing it, and above all to co-operate with the provincial government. I point out to the minister that it will be a lot easier to get co-operation from the provincial government now as there will be an election in that province shortly. There is nothing like the prospect of an election to cause a government in office to discover that they must now co-operate with Ottawa on even so-called impossible miracles, because the official opposition is on their heels and crowding them. I urge the minister to strike when the iron is hot, and it is plenty hot right now, in order to get those two large Vancouver projects out of the deep freeze before it is too late.
Federal spending on housing must be focused on public housing. I wish to quote from page 25 of the minister's speech:
My particular concern then is for the low income group. It is my intention that the capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation- the direct federal investment in housing-will be devoted to the special programs for low income families, the elderly, and the disadvantaged-
Having read that far, I was thinking that this was grand. But then I read the rest of the sentence:
-to a greater extent than in any previous year.
That is when the balloon collapsed because in previous years the support from the federal government for public housing was pitiful. If the minister cannot raise his sights higher
National Housing Act
than that at the beginning of his job, I am afraid he will not be able to deal with the pressures caused by the need for public housing. The truth of the matter is that those in the middle and upper income groups have been able to profit very largely from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, those in the $6,500 and lower income groups cannot be helped by larger and longer term mortgages. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation simply must help this group.
I wish to point out three reasons why we cannot afford the luxury of slums. One reason is that slums lead to blighted lives. This country is littered with people who have led blighted lives and who have not had any chance to improve themselves because they were born in slums and still live in slums. In some cases they are already second, third or fourth generation slums.
The second reason we cannot afford the luxury of slums is that they are the seed-bed of poor citizenship. We need only look to our neighbours to the south to see what happens when slums are allowed to grow and ghettos to proliferate.
The third reason we cannot afford this luxury is that it involves the unnecessary spending of cold, hard cash. Some years ago I visited Seattle's first public housing project, Yesler Way. I called on a university professor who had done more than anyone else to cut through the red tape in order to make Yesler Way possible. I asked him the secret of his success in getting this project off the ground. He told me he had had a survey made in this slum area of the cost to the municipality of police protection, delinquency, crime, extra educational measures and all the services necessary where slums exist. He also had had a similar survey made of another district in that city, a comfortable middle-class neighbourhood. When he put the two cost sheets in front of the business community of Seattle they realized that slums were a luxury they could no longer afford. This is how Seattle's first public housing project got off the ground.
The business community and Canada as a whole cannot afford to tolerate slums. Housing must be made a public utility. Anything short of this approach will fall far short of the needed requirements in slum areas. It is true that condominium housing is possible for some of those in the $6,500 income bracket. I hope condominium housing will be pushed wherever there is a possibility of doing so.
I wish to point out to the minister that people in the $6,500 bracket can at best afford to pay no more than $100 a month, $75 for

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
the actual rent and $25 for upkeep and repairs. This means they cannot afford a mortgage of over $16,000 and they require a 40-year term. They cannot afford to pay more than 4 per cent interest on a mortgage. Where are these people going to get mortgages at 4 per cent? In the United States, the Scandinavian countries-I don't know where the scoffers at Sweden are today-and in some other countries public housing loans are provided at interest rates as low as 4 per cent. They could also be provided in this country if the minister would accept the suggestion made by my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) that legislation be enacted directing banks, mortgage companies and other lending institutions to divert a stated percentage of their portfolio into housing loans at a 4 per cent rate of interest. They will not do this because they want to, but for the same reason we pay taxes and keep the lids on our garbage cans, because it is the law. They will not do it because of moral suasion, any other kind of suasion or appeals to their better nature. They will do it only if it becomes mandatory.
These are some of the facts which must be faced if we are going to provide housing for those people who are not in a position to provide it for themselves. These facts must be faced. I realize this is a mighty tough job to have suddenly dumped in one's lap, even if one is young and vigorous and baton twirling as the minister is doing at the moment. I do not blame the minister for doing that. It is much better than smoking.
Home ownership is possible in condominiums. I think the idea of renovating older homes is very good. My colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), will be dealing with that subject. It will be of great use in Vancouver and other centres. Home ownership of actual houses would also be possible on this basis in country districts, in small hamlets and villages.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
But the biggest mistake the task force made, if one can find it and I believe I have, is that it did not realize the truth that in 1969 the dream cottage surrounded by roses and owned by its occupants is not a possibility for the vast majority of people living in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, Quebec City, Ottawa and other cities. The former minister was reluctant to believe that truth with the result that he threw out the baby with the bath water. He panicked when he realized

how far short our public housing projects fall from what they should be and put them all in the deep freeze.
I now want to deal with low rental projects, and the things we must avoid in future when we are considering them. We have to plan such projects well. We cannot have any more concrete mausoleums set in canyons of cement. I do not want to see any more projects like Raymur in Vancouver designed for families.

I know the former minister agrees. This is why he threw out the baby with the bathwater. He knew that in such projects babies could fall from high balconies or windows and be killed. I know that the low cost rental project in downtown Vancouver where elderly people are to live is fine because they can use elevators, and they do not put their feet six feet up to make marks on the doors, as sometimes happens in projects where families are living with children.
These projects must be planned with a view to the people who are going to live in them. I believe that 350 people to a project is the outside limit suggested by a number of housing experts. These projects must have variety and be provided with a number of other amenities. One of the greatest lacks in these projects has been the lack of recreational facilities and planned recreational activities.
The minister knows that I have been particularly critical about such projects as Skee-na Terrace in Vancouver, and Orchard Park and Little Mountain, but I have not been nearly so critical of MacLean Park because by the time construction of it started the authorities began to put in such facilities. We must have activity rooms in these projects. If we had activity rooms there would be far less tearing around by young people, ruining the buildings, spoiling the hallways and the doorways.
Not too long ago I visited the Bayshore housing development, a private project on the outskirts of Ottawa. There I found a very nice community centre as part of the project, containing rooms for elderly people, rumpus rooms for the young, meeting rooms, games rooms and other facilities. I have not heard of any disturbances at Bayshore, of riots, race or otherwise. The people there have planned living facilities. They are good tenants and are comfortable.
I suggest that when we get around to incorporating the same sort of thing in our public
May 30, 1969

projects we shall have the same sort of tenants. It may take a while to build up that type of morale in tenants. You do not suddenly take people out of poor areas and put them into very good areas without some kind of trouble. But as the chief public housing architect of Oslo, Norway, told me in that city many years ago, they found there that each generation removed from the slums improved over the preceding one in manners and behavior in public housing.
In the city of Vancouver the tenants of all the public housing projects have established the Vancouver Housing Inter-Project Council which has set to work to make recommendations for future public housing projects. Here are some of the things they recommend regarding activity rooms. The first is a large meeting room with a kitchenette and washroom, to be subdivided and used as a multipurpose room. The second is a large rumpus room for young people. The third is a preschool playroom with adjacent fenced area to be used as a tot lot. The fourth is a community workshop, particularly for apartment dwellers. A basement room with a workbench should be made available to tenants. There is such a room in one of our low rental projects in Vancouver and I can assure the minister that it is used. The fifth recommendation is that a sitting room should be available for senior citizens preferably in their own part of the apartment building. Finally, they say that a community office is also desirable, which could be used by a variety of people and various workers for private interviews, etc.
These are the types of facilities required to save public housing projects from being the sort of things that frightened the wits out of the former minister in charge of housing. I say that I do not blame him for being frightened when he saw these projects. I suggest that such facilities should be built into existing housing projects that were not properly planned in the first place.
In addition to activity rooms inside there should be outside facilities for recreation. There should be playing fields. There should be other facilities for young folk, for teenage activities, where they can enjoy themselves with proper supervision. I can think of Orchard Park in my own riding where there are no properly directed outdoor activities for young people. The result is that senior citizens who occupy a part of the project, small, low, single storey dwellings, are often wakened by what they regard as young hellions scrambling over the roofs, and the windows of these dwellings are liable to be broken by
National Housing Act
balls when games are played outside them. Mothers of children in that project are frantic because there are no proper play facilities for their children. This sort of thing should be avoided. There should be proper outdoor playing space provided for the young people.
With regard to Skeena Terrace and the provision of such outdoor recreational facilities, no doubt in years gone by the responsible minister said, "This is a ridiculous thing to ask for because there is no room outside." Of course there is no room. Skeena Terrace and other public housing projects were erected on the worst possible sites that no one else wanted for anything. Skeena Terrace is located on three arterial highways with no proper means of transport for the tenants to get to stores, to church, or to other places that people want to go.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, there is no playing space at Skeena Terrace. But let me tell the minister that there is something that could be done to improve the situation there. Right across from Skeena Terrace there is a large public park. In the corner of that park nearest to Skeena Terrace a large community centre could be built which would serve not only Skeena Terrace but Beulah Gardens, a nearby low rental project for old people. These projects are in the constituency of my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East.
The trouble about building such a community centre is that under the present division of jurisdiction it is the responsibility of the city, and the city simply cannot afford to put up a community centre on that very nice park site. Since the minister is ready to seek and extend co-operation, since the electoral circumstances are favourable for getting the cooperation of the Premier of British Columbia, and since the city of Vancouver is just itching to get some help to build a community centre on that side, I suggest that it would be a very good time for the minister to go out there, sit down with the provincial minister in charge of housing, Dan Campbell, and the city authorities, and try to get this community centre under way. I think this could be done, and that centre would provide several other things that the people in the public housing project need.
Once built the community centre would weld the public housing tenants into the community. It would do away with the ghetto status of Skeena Terrace. It could be the focus for activity programs. Instead of having to pay the whole shot for outside recreational

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
areas and activity programs indoors and out, the minister could co-operate with the parks board of the city of Vancouver so that the community center could share in supplying workers to provide activity programs for the elderly people in Beulah Gardens and for the people, young and old, in Skeena Terrace.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
Do you see what I mean? This is the modern approach. When we talk about modern streamlined efficiency I think this means meeting the needs of people who cannot look after themselves and not those people who can look after themselves. If you will not do it on ethical grounds, for goodness sake remember that a mansion sits uneasy in the midst of a slum and that a healthy Canadian community cannot sit easy in the midst of the rotted downtown cores of our big cities.
I know I do not have very much time but there are a few other things I should like to mention. Mr. Minister, if you will undertake the rehabilitation of the whole concept of how to deal with low cost housing you will be able to change pariahs into participants; you will give the people in low rent housing something to live for, some link with the rest of the community instead of being cut off. Another thing I think you might take a look at, Mr. Minister, while you are fresh in office in this. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation projects have a rent geared to income policy. I agree with that policy, but it should now be geared to income, plus.
There is a plus of $50 and if tenants' incomes increase by more than $50 their rent goes up. If you want to provide incentives- today we talk about incentives on every hand and there is a danger of losing them-do increase that $50 limit somewhat. If you do so this will permit the people in public housing projects to get the training they need from manpower and other sources and to go out and obtain a job. When they have jobs and are established in them, then you can take them out of there and make the public housing available for people who really need help.
I urge you to do this because all across Canada there are many people-and I know them personally in my own city-in these housing projects who would like nothing better than to become trained, find work and get out. But they do not do that because the minute they start earning a little wee bit their rent goes up and for that reason they cannot afford to get out and earn. They need a little leeway in order to get established. I wish

you, Mr. Minister, would look at that situation to see whether we could get them trained so that they could earn.
This is participatory democracy. Participatory democracy is said to be the keynote now. It does not consist of the brass flitting about on beautiful journeys across this country to see how the grass lives and then coming back and making plans concerning what is good Tor the grass. Participatory democracy consists of the people who are doing the planning and building having the courage to take the initiative to take the action required in the lives of these people. Heaven knows we have had enough surveys. The task force conducted a great many surveys and interviews in addition to all the other surveys which have been going on. We know what is required and need no more surveys in order to make a start. If you do need surveys, I can tell you one place to get information. That is from the people who actually live in these housing projects. They are the ones who know the situation.
So please, Mr. Minister, before we make up our minds about you and while our minds are still open-and obviously my mind is wide open because you have not done anything yet and have not had an opportunity to do so-before we give vent to any preconceived prejudices of any kind or form any newly conceived ones, please take action of the right kind and you will earn our undying gratitude and that of the people all across Canada. We know you have the interests of the people at heart, but for goodness sake, if you really intend to cope with the problem of housing forget your friends, those who surround you, all those comfortable people, and keep your eye on the ball-in this case the people with incomes of $6,500 or less.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT, 1954   AMENDMENTS CLARIFYING DEFINITIONS AND DEALING WITH THE INTEREST RATE ON INSURED LOANS, AND OTHER MATTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my major purpose in rising to participate in this debate is not to praise the government for proposing Bill C-192, nor is it to laud those supplementary policies enunciated Wednesday by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) responsible for housing notwithstanding that I realize that many attractive and badly needed features have been advanced as amendments to the National Housing Act. Neither is it my intention this afternoon to expound upon the whole range of problems dealing with the housing issue. This would be a repetitious exercise, the entire spectrum of housing already having received extensive and varied comment. However, I do wish to make or remake, as the case may be, a few salient points which
May 30. 1969

are tempered by the views of one who represents a large rural riding, that of Okanagan-Kootenay, dealing with a few of the peculiar problems that are being encountered in such a region.
Firstly, it is my contention that the government should give top priority to the problems of rural area residents and in particular make more N.H.A. funds available to those who reside in the relatively small communities therein. I submit that all people in rural areas should be afforded the opportunity of participating in federal housing loans, be they residents of municipalities or unorganized territories. Their lot should not be discounted in the light of the problems inherent in the larger urban centres. I suggest that present government policy and support regulations are directed in the main to the benefit of major population centres and to the detriment of the many thousands of our citizens situate in rural areas. For too long too large a proportion of available mortgage funds has been allocated to the large cities of Canada for the propagation of multi-million dollar apartment buildings and like projects. This imbalance should be rectified and the government should cultivate a willingness on the part of private financial institutions to place funds in more remote regions by itself overcoming an apparent reluctance to invest needed capital in places of rural habitation.
Contrary to lingering government thinking, a home to those living in Vernon, Armstrong, Sicamous, Revelstoke, Golden, Invermere, Kimberley, Cranbrook, Jaffray, Elko, Fernie, Sparwood and so many other smaller centres in my constituency, is no less important than is the necessity of accommodation for the folk of Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal. May I suggest that the principal ogre perpetuating this inequality in lending policy is C.M.H.C.'s present regulation requiring the construction of piped services to housing. In a phrase: No water or sanitary sewer, therefore no eligibility for N.H.A. financed loans. Although there are stated exceptions to this rule, in my experience leniency in their interpretation has never been the federal corporation's watchword. And there are many areas in this country, and Okanagan-Kootenay is representative, that will never be serviced with piped sewer and water. So, at the moment, hundreds of people living in unorganized portions of my riding and several thousand more who reside within municipal boundaries are effectively shut out from public assistance because they are on wells and/ or septic tanks. And for those who intend to 29180-588
National Housing Act
locate and build, to join their fellow primary producers, or take their employment in the extractive industries, the same fate awaits them.
Facilities which are entirely satisfactory to many of my people, and have been for years are still effectively quite unacceptable to the crown corporation. Moreover, even though modern technology has provided us with a number of more sophisticated and proven sewage disposal systems, C.M.H.C. has steadfastly refused to accept them, and as a result of these overly restrictive regulations it is impossible for many and too tough fof most to comply.
I therefore say that, even though I share the concern of all levels of government for the pollution of ground and water, which concern undoubtedly has given birth to these constrictions, and even though I am quite aware that the use of septic tanks in concentration will create difficulties in curbing pollution, surely a workable set of regulations which would supplant those that have outlived their usefulness can be formulated which would then permit the use of certain lands, presently exempt from mortgage financing, and a goodly portion of which will never be equipped with piped services, on a septic disposal and water well basis. Such a solution would inject a new and needy borrower into the program and would also raise the generally low standard of housing prevalent in sections of our country, certainly in several of the more depressed portions of my riding.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
On another matter, although Bill C-192 makes an attempt to assist those on small or fixed incomes, the 20 per cent of the people either below or hovering on the poverty level, I am not convinced that the intended modifications go far enough. Even though the amortization period for loans now permissible is to be extended, and although the amount of mortgage money is about to be increased to $18,000 for improvement and purchase of used homes, both of which amendments are commendable, are we still doing all we can to aim our policy toward assisting that class of people below the subsistence level or, for that matter, toward the average wage earner? I think not. Moreover, I think that the lack of any effective means to control rent, coupled with today's high cost of money, simply precludes these classes of Canadians from enjoying what every Canadian should be able to enjoy-reasonable accommodation.

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
Whether a solution takes the form, as suggested in the Task Force report, of implementing a program of income supplements to permit low income families and those on fixed incomes to rent or even purchase housing according to their own needs, whether the government institutes a policy whereby, in certain cases, interest payments on home mortgages are wholly or partially income tax deductible, or whether interest rates on mortgages are set on a graduating scale depending on the size of the mortgage, thus encouraging less expensive homes and assisting lower income groups, there must be some better solution than that proposed. I urge the government to find one along these lines.
My third point this afternoon relates to the tremendous and stifling amount of red tape which one encounters and attempts to cut a swath through in his dealings with both the department and its agency responsible for housing. If I may be forgiven for again being parochial, I would like to cite the Sparwood land assembly program at present under way in my riding as but one example.
Approximately four and a half years ago it was determined by the provincial government that an urban renewal program should be put into effect for the Michel-Natal townsites. The municipality, on agreeing to such a scheme, requested that a land assembly be formed some four miles away in Sparwood. This area, as hon. members may know, is the region where the massive Kaiser coal development is now in its initial stages. It is some 38 miles from where the proposed Fording Coal operations are anticipated. In excess of some 500 additional housing units are urgently required for miners and for those people serving in an ancillary capacity.
Everyone directly concerned with this development, including the municipality and the coal company, has to my knowledge diligently pursued in every conceivable manner the frustrating task of attempting to traverse the maze of regulations and format restricting progress. The scheme is still off the rails, although admittedly success is now within reasonable reach. The problem? I do not really know, but I would strongly suggest that it is certainly one demanding an immediate solution.
Before I leave this subject I must say a word about the apparent unavailability of adequate mortgage financing in the south eastern portion of Okanagan-Kootenay. I am advised that the Kaiser Company has attempted in every foreseeable, proper way to get contractors to build permanent homes

as well as single dwelling units. I am told that developers with as much as 40 per cent equity have requested loans from C.M.H.C., banks and other lending institutions and have been advised that it was not desirable to invest money in this area. Of course the lending institutions were somewhat more willing to listen to the housing problems if Kaiser would guarantee the mortgages. But the company, although it has undertaken to develop 50 lots, is not in the housing business; it is in the coal mining business. Concurrently the company attempted to get contractors who already had loans in existence with C.M.H.C. to build apartments, but I am again, advised that C.M.H.C. had no funds available for this purpose in the Fernie-Sparwood area.
The whole point? It appears that there is great governmental concern over the alleged risk involved in putting public funds into this region. The region until recently was, admittedly, somewhat impoverished and depressed but it is a region now, I suggest, which has its future guaranteed, without risk. However, it is still a region that urgently requires a more relaxed housing policy which would enable it to obtain and utilize the mortgage funds it so desperately needs now.
On a final point, Mr. Speaker, in an effort to obtain the ideas and proposals of interested and concerned individuals and organizations in my riding in respect of the housing issue, I had occasion last October to write every mayor, regional district chairman, chamber of commerce, M.L.A. and real estate agency in Okanagan-Kootenay. The response to my solicitations was excellent.
For the benefit of the minister and the committee to which this bill will shortly be referred for deliberation, I would like at this point, in capsule form, to recite a number of the more important recommendations I received in response to my request. They are as follows:
1.	There exists a definite need for both greater mechanization in house building and for further research into more efficient materials and methods of construction. The National Research Council should intensify its research into the use of new materials such as fiberglass, for structural components, and other labour-saving techniques.
2.	The government should encourage more efficient utilization of land through development of rural housing and make financing readily available for such projects under condominium ownership.
May 30, 1969

3.	Lower interest rates are required on housing loans, especially insured loans.
4.	Eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials for houses costing up to $25,000.
5.	Greater assistance is required in developing skilled tradesmen in the construction field.
6.	Relax the requirements for and encourage the development of more senior citizens low rental housing projects.
7.	Encourage development of leasehold land for home construction.
8.	Investigate present C.M.H.C. and National Building Code standards with the idea of updating these rules relative to modern materials and methods.
9.	Consumer education should be provided by senior levels of government on the desirability of erecting basementless houses, with resulting construction cost reductions.
10.	The government should extend National Housing Act authority allowing moneys to be made available to municipal governments, as well as private corporations, for the development of residential subdivisions.
Mr. Speaker and hon. members, other than offering my own good wishes to the new minister I have nothing further to add at this time on the subject of housing. I thank all hon. members for listening attentively to my submissions.

municipalities in working to improve housing and urban conditions since the last war. It is quite true that at various points precedents were set and new departures were made. Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by making some comments which perhaps may help in the consideration of some of the points which have been raised thus far by opposition speakers in the debate and give a broader perspective to them in a way that I hope will aid in consideration of this very important bill. And this is a bill to which I give my entire support.
Reference has been made to the effect of the federal sales tax on building materials on building costs. But some, I submit, who comment on this effect greatly overestimate the impact of this tax. The rate of federal sales

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
tax on most building materials is 11 per cent. That does not mean that it adds 11 per cent to the cost of a house. The amount an individual pays for his home includes cost of land, legal fees and the cost of construction. A substantial part of the cost of construction is in the area of labour costs. But only the materials used in constructing the house bear sales tax on their price. The tax is imposed when the materials are sold by the manufacturer and not at the price the builder pays. Therefore, taking all these factors into consideration, it has been estimated that the present federal sales tax on building materials may add between 3 per cent and 4 per cent to the actual cost of construction.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has said on a previous occasion and as I said during a late show debate not long ago when speaking on his behalf, one must recognize the hard fact that if important tax reductions were made at the present time the public would either have to pay the same amount of tax in some other way or go without some service or benefit which it has come to expect from the government.
Estimates based on the value of production of building materials and related statistics lead to the conclusion that the sales tax on all building materials now yields over $300 million a year. The revenue from materials used in the construction of housing of all kinds is more difficult to estimate but is believed to be in the area of between $130 million and $140 million. Therefore if the entire sales tax on building materials were to be repealed at this time, obviously some equivalent measure of taxation would have to be introduced to replace it.
An exemption on building materials used only in housing would, of course, involve lower amounts, but the sales tax not obtained thereby would still have to be obtained from other sources. Also, it would be very difficult to administer an exemption restricted to building materials used only for housing construction. As we know, Mr. Speaker, the tax is paid by the manufacturer of materials. He does not know whether the bricks, lumber or glass he produces will be used to build a house or factory. It certainly would not be an easy task to differentiate between residential and non-residential use.
No good answer has ever been given as to why the sales tax on construction material should be eliminated right across the board including, for example, the tax on materials

used in the construction of luxury office towers or luxury apartments. Speaking personally, therefore, I think it would be better to look at this matter in terms of rebates of sales tax to purchasers of low-priced homes, those selling below a certain price.
The other day, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) said that the proposed amendments to the income tax legislation contained in Bill C-191, which alter the method of taxing insurance companies, would have an adverse effect on the supply of mortgage funds in Canada. I believe the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) who spoke a moment ago made the same comment. These hon. members suggested that since these changes increase the tax on insurance companies to some $90 million and since half of the funds of these companies is invested in mortgages, the change would cause a decrease of $45 million in mortgage funds.
While the new tax could have some effect on the amount of funds invested by insurance companies in mortgages, it should be noted that the managements of these companies are not willing to say yet exactly to what extent they will react to the proposed changes. I therefore find it difficult to see how the hon. members who have made statements to the effect that there will be a reduction in the availability of mortgage funds to the extent they have mentioned can make those statements so definitely at this time.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, one could argue that the new tax revenue coming from this tax on insurance companies could help the government to make greater amounts of funds available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing loans and subsidies than it might otherwise be able to do. Such action would certainly tend to offset any decrease in mortgage investments by life insurance companies. In any event, the amount of $45 million is not that much when compared with the total new investment in mortgage loans, which in 1968 amounted to some $2.7 billion. Also, while the possible effect on the supply of mortgage funds is important it should be remembered that the main purpose of these tax changes is to bring the taxation of the insurance industry into line with the taxation of other investment institutions and thereby improve the equity of our tax system.
I believe the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) made some suggestions about passing legislation to compel financial intermediaries or financial institutions to put a certain proportion of their investments into

mortgages. I think it should be stressed that the federal government is interested in having a greater supply of mortgage funds from the private sector, but the federal government has up to now and is continuing to put its emphasis on creating conditions which will encourage financial institutions to invest more in mortgages for homes. It will also continue its efforts based on discussion and consultation.
I am told that mortgage companies and trust companies at the present time have about 80 per cent of their investments in mortgages. This exemption will bear heavily on the general population which has to provide the funds for paying the interest and service charges on these bonds. If such bonds were issued and put on the market, they would compete for investment funds with other types of securities. This may have the effect of increasing interest rates. And concern has often been expressed in this house about high interest rates.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) suggested that mortgage interest should be deductible from income tax. This type of proposal has been made many times in the past-that home owners should be allowed to deduct municipal tax payments and mortgage home payments from taxable income for income tax purposes. Advocates of this proposal usually point out landlords are allowed to do this with regard to properties they rent to others and therefore homeowners should be allowed to do the same. While this argument seems superficially attractive, there are weaknesses in it. It is true landlords are allowed to consider interest and other charges such as depreciation, however, they are obliged under our tax laws to consider rental payments as revenue. This law does not apply to homeowners.
If this law were changed and the homeowner had to report as income the rent he pays as a tenant on his own property, perhaps then the argument might be made more strongly that he should be able to claim as deductions from income tax costs items such as the payments he makes for mortgage interest. At the present time he is not obliged to report as income what he pays in rent or in effect the investment income he has from living in his own property. The argument might be made in reply therefor that he should not be allowed to claim the costs.
It is interesting to note as I have said that the proposal to which I referred has been mentioned on a number of occasions in the past. The Carter Royal Commission put forward a number of grounds for rejecting it. I will not go over all these grounds, but I want

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
to put on the record that the Carter Commission stated in part such a deduction would be of value to homeowners only and would provide no relief for persons who rent their accommodation. This would put the latter group at a considerable disadvantage. This is of some significance as a prime proportion of the low income group rent their accommodation.
Perhaps some of these thoughts may help in consideration of the points to which they are directed, points which are certainly worthy of consideration in the context of this debate. The federal government has been working to give leadership and assistance in the field of housing, particularly since the end of the second world war. The report of the federal task force on housing pointed out that: "more than one-third of the total national production of housing since 1945 has been carried out" because of federal activity in support of housing. In 1968, 196,800 housing units were started and 210,000' are forecast for this year. If this rate continues, the target called for by the Economic Council of Canada and by the task force to fill Canada's housing needs for the 1965-70 period will clearly be met. It appears, looking at the rate of starts in the first quarter of this year, compared with the rate for the fourth quarter of last year, a rate which is much higher, the results in housing of last year will be substantially exceeded in 1969. It is more than likely that this year will again be a record one for residential construction.
These figures help us to keep this question in perspective. It could be said this activity has certainly been stimulated by the additional measures taken by the federal government last year which have been added to the other measures it has put into effect during the past five years.
As an example of what this meant for one particular urban community, let us look for a moment at what this has meant for housing starts in my own Windsor area. There were only 495 in 1962 but in 1968 there were 1,469, the best year since 1965. In the first three months of 1969 there were more than 1,100 housing starts compared with some 200 or so in the first three months of last year.
If one looks at public housing in Windsor, including senior citizens' units there were 909 in existence in 1963. Today, there are 1,691. Under construction at present are 557 units for senior citizens, with a call out for proposals for the construction of a further 200 family units. This increase in public housing has 
been made possible in my opinion largely through the stimulus of federal government measures implemented in the last five years. And yet, in spite of these efforts and what they have brought about, there still is not a supply of decent housing at a reasonable cost sufficient to meet the demand for it in Canada today-a demand reflecting our rapid urban growth in recent years.
The director of research for the city of Windsor, Mr. C. T. Ouellette, has recently conducted a survey which shows applications for 835 family units and 919 senior citizen units on the active waiting list for public housing in Windsor today. Similar examples can be gathered from almost every urban area of any size in Canada. Obviously, there is certainly more that has to be done. The Canadian people understandably are calling for further action. I think that in presenting this bill at this time the federal government is responding in a positive way to this call for action. Its aim is to help bring about a significant improvement in the supply of homes for Canadians.
Let me touch briefly on some of the changes it covers. A number of them in the bill or in the regulations, I expect, will help more people to be in a position to buy their own homes, people who could not afford to consider doing so before. It provides for increases in maximum loans for both new and older homes, with the effect of lowering the down payment and lessening the need for expensive second mortgage financing. There is an increase in the maximum amortization period to 40 years. This will help bring about lower monthly payments. The reduction of the mortgage insurance fee by 50 per cent will certainly bring about a reduction in cost.
A needed and important change is the increase in maximum loans for older homes. This will help eliminate second mortgage financing which adds to the cost. This step helps bring home ownership more within the means of people with lower incomes who are more likely to be able to afford the prices at which older homes are offered.
This provision, together with another making possible federal loans for the acquisition and rehabilitation of existing homes in urban renewal areas, will help bring about a more effective use of our existing supply of housing. All this means that more of the new homes that are being build will be bringing about an absolute increase in our housing stock instead of simply replacing houses which are torn down during urban renewal, as was the case all too often before.

The removal of the provision tying the ceiling on interest rates for N.H.A. mortgages to rates for short term federal borrowing is aimed at encouraging more private funds to be available for home mortgages. It is hoped that by letting the rate find levels based on market forces there will no longer be the same drying up of funds for housing mortgages that used to come about from time to time in the past, when lenders found more attractive opportunities elsewhere. At the same time one looks forward to the government's anti-inflationary measures bringing about a downward pressure on interest rates. And one should not overlook the fact that another recent change in the regulations provides a five year roll-over for N.H.A. mortgages, enabling the borrower at the end of the five years to seek a more advantageous rate if it is available at that time.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The bill rightly reflects the government's desire to give first priority in its policy to meeting the housing needs of low income groups. And the government is therefore also rightly applying this same priority in the way it will be carrying out its own program of direct lending and subsidy payments for housing.
It is extending the bounds within which it will make loans for limited dividend projects, and projects developed by non-profit organizations. There will be much greater scope for action in this field. It will help take care of the needs of people whose incomes may be somewhat above the limits of eligibility for public housing but who are not yet able to find decent housing in the open market, something seen quite frequently in the Windsor area.
These changes provide new opportunities for trade unions, churches, employee pension funds and industrial firms to develop projects with fixed lower levels of rental, and also co-operative housing projects such as the new Solidarity Tower project now being built in Windsor under the auspices of the Union of Automobile Workers with the help of a direct federal loan.
The government was certainly wise in recognizing that the immediate need for shelter for the lower income groups transcended the importance of dealing with the social problems that appear to have been created by the methods of developing public housing previously in use. It is proceeding to allow public housing projects, which had been sufficiently developed so as to be on the verge of
National Housing Act
construction, to proceed, and at the same time it is taking a wise step by going on to work out new approaches to try to eliminate some of the stigma, the social difficulties, that all too often have been attached in the minds of some to living in public housing projects.
Also the willingness of the federal government to share now with the provinces in the cost of acquiring or renting existing units for public housing purposes, will mean a more effective use of existing stock, as well as a step toward lessening the setting apart of people in subsidized housing from the rest of the community.
The increase in the maximum mortgage to $18,000 for older homes will also open the way to an extent not possible before for tenants in public housing units, particularly those whose incomes have gone to or above the maximum to purchase the units in which they live, another matter of great interest to housing in the Windsor area.
An important factor in the present cost of housing is the excessively high cost of serviced land, and its shortage as well, in our urban areas. The bill makes possible a new form of federal action to help tackle this problem. It will make possible loans to provinces or municipalities-I presume with provincial approval-or to provincial housing agencies, of 90 per cent of the cost of acquiring and servicing land, and this land will then be available not only for the building of public housing but now for the first time for private housing as well. These loans, to be made at a preferential rate and for 15 years, should help lower the cost of homes built on land assembled in this way. The existence of such publicly owned land assembly developments should also, through competitive pressure, help hold back the cost of lots on privately assembled land, and therefore the cost of homes built on them.
This measure illustrates how the federal government is in a position to accomplish more in the field of housing at the present time, by taking into account the realities of our present constitution. Under this constitution, over the years, housing has been considered to be essentially under provincial jurisdiction. Certainly problems connected with it, and other urban matters as well, cannot be dealt with by the federal government alone, or solely under its direction. There are many areas of concern which affect the supply and cost of housing which can be dealt with only by the provincial governments and the municipalities.

May 30, 1969
National Housing Act
Examples of these are matters of zoning, planning assessment and building codes. Now' there is need for action in these areas and this action can come only from provincial governments. There is room for more provincial initiative in these and other areas of policy and administration in the field of urban affairs. There is room for more provincial initiative, at the very least, in taking advantage of financial assistance made available by the federal government for housing to the maximum possible degree-something that has not always been the case in the past-in every province of Canada.
To be effective, to get real results today the federal government's method and scope of action must take into account our existing constitutional arrangements. It is not a matter of getting bogged down in "constitutional niceties" or, as some have claimed, in "hiding behind the constitution", but instead, of a facing up to and a dealing with "constitutional realities". And these realities are that our present constitution exists in a certain form. Until it is changed if we want to get anything done right now in the field of housing, or for that matter in any field of activity requiring some form of government support or intervention, we have to be aware of and work within its framework.
If, and as I think it should, the federal government is to do more than it has been doing until now in the field of housing and on other matters of concern to our cities, then it cannot simply ignore our present constitution. If the federal government attempted to do so the results would be confusion, negative confrontation and complications-certainly not the most effective use of taxpayers' money. In other words, more constitutional court cases perhaps, but not more housing.
At the same time when it comes to housing and urban affairs generally, the federal government should exercise its existing constitutional jurisdiction as fully and as creatively as possible. And to the extent that this jurisdiction is lacking, it must then, through cooperation and consultation with the provinces, work out with them arrangements whereby they would exercise their own jurisdiction to fill in the gaps. This co-operative approach has already been used with success in recent years on a number of occasions. It is being used by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) and by the government at the present time to move toward the essential goal of decent housing at reasonable cost for all Canadians.

I should mention, however, that it could be that no matter how creatively used, the present constitution may not enable effective solutions to be found for all current problems. Therefore, while federal and provincial governments are doing what they can to fill the needs of Canadians under the existing constitution, it is in the meantime of real importance to increase the pace of discussions on its reform and change.
Shakespeare once wrote, "The people are the city." Today 75 per cent of our people live in our urban areas. With the continuing trends in this direction it could well come to be said that "Canada is the city," because that is where its people will be. This federal government therefore, if it is to continue to be a meaningful and relevant government for the Canadian people in days to come, cannot fail to be increasingly involved, within its jurisdiction, in finding solutions to the problems of urban life. The biff before us today shows how the government is responding in a positive way to this need for involvement.

Mr. Speaker, in his speech on Wednesday, the hon. minister responsible for housing placed particular emphasis on housing for low income Canadians. His decision will certainly help in alleviating their present condition. I believed that the minister's priorities have given housing new momentum and Canadians new hope. I shall speak today about Metro Toronto because it is the city I know best, but I have no doubt that similar situations are occurring now or will occur in the future in other parts of Canada. I intend to speak mainly about public housing.
Two years ago a research study of housing needs was commissioned by the metropolitan Toronto planning board. Because of the complexity of the subject matter and the changing conditions of the housing market, this study was completed only in March of this year. This study reveals that for the period starting in 1966 and ending in 1981 there will be a need for approximately 95,000 public housing units in Metro Toronto. This figure is in respect of families of three or more persons with an income of up to $5,640 per annum and experiencing one of four housing inadequcies. The first is an inadequacy resulting from poor structural conditions either alone or in combination with overcrowding. The second is an inadequacy due to poor condition and occupancy by one or more families, either with or without overcrowding. The third is an inadequacy due to occupancy by two or more families, with or without overcrowding, and the fourth is an inadequacy due to overcrowding alone.
This estimated need of 95,000 public housing units was surprisingly high and it required careful study. A criterion was developed for this purpose. They called it the

National Housing Act
effective demand ratio. This is the proportion of the total number of eligible families who have applied for public housing and who would accept it when offered to them. This ratio, however, is subject to change. It depends on the availability and acceptance of public housing, on the waiting period, on the choice of location, on the type of dwelling, and also on public awareness. At present it is approximately one to three, which means that one of every three families on the waiting list would accept housing when offered. This ratio is important to planners, administrators, and politicians if they are to forecast the needs for public housing. Perhaps it is important enough to warrant a study under the auspices of C.M.H.C.
After having applied this ratio to the number of public housing dwelling units needed in Metro Toronto for the ten year period from 1971 to 1981, the report recommended 3,500 dwelling units per year over a period of ten years at a cost of $56 million per year in 1969 values. This recommended long term provision of 35,000 dwelling units of public housing for Metro Toronto would go only part way to meeting the housing goals of the report.
The report states that there are 47,000 families who would not apply for public housing but who would still be living beyond their means and in inadequate housing. It also reported that there are a further 134,500 families in middle and lower income brackets who would be unable to afford adequate housing in the open market but would not qualify for public housing under present policies.

I refer to low cost, low down payment, condominium projects as at present proposed, and others. Two other factors make the metro Toronto situation rather unique. In his closing remarks on Wednesday, the minister welcomed suggestions. I shall try to submit a few on the subject of public housing. But before doing so, Mr. Speaker, allow me to look for a moment at the success the private housing industry has had in the provision of apartment buildings. What are the reasons? They are probably these: No. 1, they are conveniently located; No. 2, rents are in fair proportion to the average income; No. 3, there is the ability to offer tenants a wide range of amenities from shopping centres to swimming pools. Our existing legislation for public housing has so far been pretty dull. If we wish to achieve a reasonably successful public housing policy in cities where land costs are almost prohibitive we can learn from the approach adopted by high-rise developers.
If our new legislation reflects the social needs of people living in public housing projects, we will be making progress. For instance, our new legislation could recognize the indispensability of day nurseries in a public housing program, of recreation rooms, of workshops for adults, of recreational areas and adequate open spaces for young people. In co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities, our new legislation could recognize the indispensability of guidance and counselling services in public housing projects in order to assist people to find their way in our rather complex urban life; it could provide guidance and information on the services offered by governments, schools and volunteer agencies, including the increasingly important question of consumers' rights. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that these services are relevant if we are to have well integrated public housing projects.
Like other major national policies, the success of a housing policy rests upon the co-operation of federal departments and other levels of government. I shall devote a few remarks to this aspect later. Investment measures aimed at reducing speculative actions were outlined on Wednesday by the minister. In addition, we must find fiscal measures
