with the same objective in mind. But this is not the only area of federal responsibility. To house Canadians we need the help of the Department of Transport to develop commuter services into our growing cities. This could sometimes be done by utilizing existing railway lines.
Another federal department which could be helpful in relation to housing is the Department of Manpower, by intensifying its efforts in attracting people to smaller Canadian cities so as to alleviate the pressure for housing in the metropolitan areas. The Department of Regional Development is already helping to bring jobs to Canadians, rather than Canadians to jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now put forward some ideas on the role other levels of government can play in housing Canadians in the coming years. The Assessment Act in the Province of Ontario is a fairly good example of the point I wish to make. It is an outdated act, rurally orientated and blissfully unaware of urban requirements. It penalizes improvements to houses except for a coat of paint; it permits the kind of land speculation we have had in metropolitan Toronto; it offers incentives to demolish buildings and convert them into parking lots, thus adding to urban congestion. Probably other provincial acts affecting housing are in need of revision.
At the municipal level, particularly in Toronto, much could be done. For instance, statistics show that during the last five years houses in Toronto have been demolished at the rate of about 1,000 dwelling units per year. Demolitions have taken place mainly to make room for high-rise buildings, schools, expressways, parking lots, and so forth. Today's housing shortage in Toronto would be a modest one had we planned to encourage high-rise buildings on vacant or commercial lots, keeping the houses we had rather than demolishing them; had we discouraged the construction of cross-town expressways and instead given impetus to public transportation in order to make it highly competitive and reduce the pressure for highways.
Here is another example. I know of one municipality which has gone so far as to prohibit two families living in houses which have a frontage of less than 40 feet. This is the effect of an incredible by-law enacted over ten years ago in the borough of York in Metro Toronto. It is a restrictive measure in times of increasing demand. This is another law at the local level which requires close scrutiny. With sufficient knowledge of the

subject, one could probably prepare a long list of pieces of legislation enacted at other levels of government which have had a negative effect on our housing policy. Perhaps each of us in this house can play a role in our own constituency and assist the minister in his efforts. But at the same time, I hope funds made available through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will become the medium to effect better planning. After all, if we are to offer the funds we should ensure that they are spent in the best possible way, and that we exercise some indirect planning powers.

Until the head of every family in Canada has at least the opportunity to own a home, one cannot say that he has either freedom or a real stake in the country. to each man to own a home. I do not think, because I am not a socialist, that it is our duty to provide that home tor him. However, in certain cases where we have made it impossible for him to provide it for himself, I think we should take emergency measures to provide temporary homes of some kind.
When I was the member for Athabasca I had 21 Indian reserves in my district, and not one of them had adequate housing. Perhaps in a situation such as this we must step into the housing field and provide shelter for these people until they obtain full citizenship rights and are able to provide it for themselves.
So far as economic ghettos in our cities are concerned, and they cannot be called anything else, we have also been neglectful in this respect. All governments can be blamed for neglect in this area. Nobody wishes to take the blame for it, but I do not want to see any more of the constitutional smokescreen being thrown up.
I have not always seen eye to eye with the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), and I do not suppose if he were to come back as minister responsible for housing I would see eye to eye with him. Nevertheless, I think he made an honest attempt to cut through the smokescreen and to let in some fresh air. At least to he took some positive and definite action by travelling across the country and talking to people who were involved. His task force came up with a report which should not be ignored. In the amendments to the act which appear in Bill C-192 the government, after having got rid of the former minister of transport, accepted the advice contained in the report of the task force and is now belatedly trying to plug some of the holes in the act. Not only should they have seriously considered the report but they should have acted on most of the recommendations contained in it. I am quite sure that even if they were not able to act on most of the recommendations because of constitutional limitations, both the provincial and municipal levels of government would have been more than 
willing to go along with a great many of the recommendations in the report.
I do not usually trot out my legal knowledge, but my main reason for taking legal training was to find out exactly what roadblocks the constitution of Canada sets up in matters like this. I can say that our constitution is sufficiently flexible to allow men of goodwill to get around any constitutional hitch there may be in our efforts to take action for the welfare of our country. It is not the constitution which is wrong but rather those people who try to use it as an obstruction and as an excuse when they are either unable or unwilling to handle the matter.
The problem does not only lie in providing enough money for housing under the N.H.A. We might use all the money in the treasury and things might still go wrong. I happen to think like the last member who spoke. I was glad to hear a member on the government side have the courage to say that not everything is well and that not all the wisdom is concentrated on the front bench opposite. I do not know whether C.M.H.C. has been allowed to use its initiative and I do not think that members of the house who have been in support of bills to provide more money for housing under the N.H.A. ever intended any of the money to go into high-priced high rise apartments. That is not the kind of emergency measure to which I am referring.
The large corporations of Canada, whether they are publicly owned or whether they are owned by the tycoons of industry, can well afford to raise money on the Canadian, the United States or the international markets, to build the high rise apartments of their choosing, with penthouses and rents ranging anywhere from $200 to $1,000 a month. They would do that no matter what C.M.H.C. says. In my opinion it would be a misuse of public money to give it to those people who already have a monopoly in the money affairs of our country. They should not be allowed to dip into the treasury.
I believe it is the intention of this parliament to make money available to the young married couples in Canada, particularly to those starting out in life who wish to own a home of their own and who do not want to be saddled with debts for the rest of their lives. There are many things that the constitution allows us to do to ensure that the explosion in the price of land is stopped. It cannot be stopped by allowing unfettered ownership and use of the land by private industry. We have restricted the so-called liberties of man

before now in cases where there have been abuses.
In my opinion, the exploitation of land adjacent to the large metropolitan areas of Canada is a standing disgrace. We are all too ready to complain about our labour unions when they go on strike for higher pay. If one has to pay $300 for rent one has to get sufficient pay somewhere, unless one is ready to steal the money. The only way that I know to get the money is to ask for more pay, but industry is not that anxious to give it to you unless you are ready to make a strong demand. I am quite sure that if we could ensure reasonable rents, there would not be so much need for strikes. The question of housing is tied in intimately with our whole economic structure, and our economic structure is tied to our so-called ideologies. "Revolution" is a word I hear bandied about. If you are a super-Conservative you join a revolution against the working man, and if you are a working man you revolt against the blue-blooded tories, and so forth. I agree with revolution, but let us have a revolution against the hidebound idea that some people do not have as much right as other people to make a decent living and to live as well as the other fellow in the country. This kind of revolution I will join.

Whether or not them methods are the right ones is another argument. However, I do not want to get into that argument today. Instead, I want to explore the housing problem. I do not think we are taking a proper look at the way to balance the economy of Canada. It is the avowed purpose of this government, it seems, to close down the small family farms. Housing is the second most important thing in life. The first is personal freedom, and the second is shelter for one's family and food on the table. Without that you have trouble.
It is to the credit of the Canadian people that we have not had far more trouble than we have. Lack of housing is something that
National Housing Act
gets into more corners than racism or language rights. For my own part I would not particularly worry which language my children spoke so long as their stomachs were full. If my children did not have food I would do almost anything to get it. I will compromise on language and culture, but I will not compromise on empty stomachs or on a system of government that deprives my children of an opportunity to be decently housed. How people can be so patient when we frustrate them, I do not know.
We do not have 20 years to think about this problem. If we do not solve it we will be replaced, and if we are not replaced we should be. Therefore, let us get down to brass tacks and make sure that the funds are available through C.M.H.C. to build houses. Let the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) not tell us there is something sacred about interest rates, because there is not. After all, money is artificial. It has no value at all except among Canadians, who honour the piece of paper on which a certain value is printed. We could have a gold standard, a timber standard or a fish standard. What the Bank of Canada does is to honour a promissory note. I think the Social Crediters are right when they say money could be made available free of interest. Under our law money could be made available at a reasonable rate of interest if we wanted to pay the price and made sure exorbitant profits were not made.
Coupled with a housing policy there must be a monetary policy, an economic policy. We must develop basic industries like farming, fishing and lumbering. We must think about conservation. If our young people want to stay on relief all summer instead of fighting forest fires, or patrolling our forests, or being surveyors, then this means we have lost our grip in terms of pioneering, of working with our hands. Under such conditions the price of housing will go up. There is no magic about this; we must have timber to build houses, and we must have it at a reasonable price.
One hon. member made the point that the sales tax on building materials does not really affect the price of a house. I submit that is patently ridiculous. I agree we must get revenue from somewhere, but I question that this is the proper place to raise it. I have never questioned the right to tax me for the liquor I drink, and I am not a teetotaller. Luxuries like this are a perfectly proper place to raise taxes. But I do not think taxing the bricks and boards with which I try to build a modest home for a modest family is the proper place.

The hon. member suggested, if I understood him correctly, that instead of the tax being 11 per cent, in effect it represented only 3 per cent on the cost of the home alone. It seems to me he is looking at the problem through the wrong end of the telescope. I suggest the 11 per cent grows to 14 per cent, 16 per cent or even 18 per cent when one thinks of mortgage cost. By the time you have finished paying off your mortgage you have paid double the value of your home. Every time you put on another tax the price increases. As I said before it is a vicious circle. If you charge your tenant too much rent, he will want too much for wages.
I have done a lot of criticizing and my suggestion is this. Having provided more money under the National Housing Act for mortgages as a stop gap measure, the government must now turn its attention to restoring the country to full employment. We must train people for employment, and this should be part of our policy. We must not put all our eggs in one basket. Since we have put more money into mortgages under the National Housing Act we might also put more money into trade training and into research.
I am glad to see that under this bill some money is set aside for research into housing. A great deal of the wealth that will come into the coffers during the next 20 years will originate north of the 60th parallel. Housing is going to be a problem in the north, perhaps forever. Money for housing will not come easily in the north. Therefore, we shall have to pick up the tab and provide housing in the north for construction workers, explorers, government employees and other people. I think that is a fair tax upon the government purse, because it is in this way that will expand the Canadian economy. Through the expenditure of a few extra hundred millions on housing we will produce more minerals, more oil, more timber and fish, as well as more security.
We cannot expect private industry to underwrite the cost of building houses at Coppermine, because as soon as the Coppermine Company has taken all of the minerals out of that area it will move on to another area, as was the case at Elliott Lake. Therefore, I suggest we should examine the possibility of providing mobile homes, or aluminum homes, properly insulated which can be taken into the north by snowmobile or tractor. Then, when a company is ready to move to the next mine these mobile homes can be rented to the next developer.

I do not think we should be so wooden about this. We should not throw up our hands and say we cannot get mortgage money, and therefore we cannot develop the north. What we require are the proper houses with the proper type of financing. Let us hear no more about northern development being impossible because our forefathers in 1867 did not understand atomic energy and other substances that are being produced at Coppermine River. We can supply the answers if only we use our brains. This is the right attitude for progress. Let us put first things first. Let us spend a little less time empire building, standing before the mirror and sitting before T.V. Let us spend a little more time solving our problems, instead of dreaming up fancy notions about why we cannot do so.

National Housing Act The Hellyer report is excellent. It was presented to us, here, in Parliament. I want to congratulate the man responsible at that time for the housing program. I believe he is a very courageous man. The work he did was tremendous in finding what we have known for five years.

wage-earner. A two percentage point increase in the same mortgage raises the monthly payment by some $19 and the total cost over 25 years by about $5,700.

cent interest rate and perhaps more, depending upon the greediness of financiers who control the Canadian economic life.

-loans without interest are the only thing that can take us out of the housing stalemate.
